citation: "Fort Dearborn II." Chicagology. Transcribing Chicago Magazine, 15 May 1857 and May 1857, and the Chicago Tribune of 27 March 1856, with a woodcut after Alexander Hesler's 1855 photograph and a lettered key.

transcribes.work: Chicago Magazine, 'Fort Dearborn II' — the account of the second fort from its re-occupation in 1816 to its demolition, written from the recollection of 'several of the oldest inhabitants, who are now permanent residents among us'
transcribes.note: Carries the fort's continuous occupation from 1832 'till the removal of the Indians in 1836' — the corroboration, independent of Andreas and of Wentworth, behind the settled finding that on 1835-07-01 Fort Dearborn was an occupied post (docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md § 3). It also carries the demolition sequence of 1856. Twenty-five to forty years after the events, from named witnesses speaking to the writer: rung 2, the same magazine and the same reading as chicagology_prefire273.

note: Worth having for the 1857 magazine text, which was written while the fort was being pulled down and by people who had watched it stand: the second fort was raised on the site of the first by Capt. Hezekiah Bradley in 1816; the troops left in May 1831 for Green Bay; it was re-occupied on the outbreak of the Black Hawk war in 1832 'and its occupancy continued till the removal of the Indians in 1836'; the officers' quarters and soldiers' barracks came down in the summer of 1856 and the block-house a few weeks after. THE THREE DIMENSIONS ON THIS PAGE ARE NOT USABLE AS EVIDENCE YET and the reason is the page's own silence: they are in the caption to a woodcut ('the parade-ground, 80x200 ft.', the commandant's quarters 'brick, about 25x50 ft.', the officers' quarters 'wood, about 30x60 ft.'), and chicagology does not say where the caption comes from. Its original has not been found. Andreas vol. 1 does not carry it. Until it is traced, nothing here may promote a dimension above conjectural, and the figure disagrees with Wentworth's parade anyway — 80 ft wide in both, 200 ft long here against 'say 400 feet' there, describing a compound twenty years apart. READ IN FULL 2026-08-11 AND REGRADED 4 → 2, ON THE DOCUMENT AND NOT ON THE HOST. The body is set under its own printed attributions — 'Chicago Magazine, May 15, 1857', then 'Chicago Magazine, May, 1857' for the Indian Agency and Cob-Web Castle passage — and it is the same magazine, and the same kind of reading, that took chicagology_prefire273 to rung 2 on 2026-08-10: written from what the oldest residents told the writer, twenty-five years after the scene this project models. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DECLARED IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF. A Chicago Tribune notice of 27 March 1856 about proposals for the purchase of the government buildings is printed below the magazine text; it is a period document and it would derive this record to rung 1. Nothing in this dataset rests on it and nothing is going to — the fort's demolition is not a claim about 1835 — so declaring it would put this record's rung on evidence the project does not stand on, which is exactly the apparatus rule. The same goes for the Hesler woodcut and its lettered key: the three dimensions in that caption remain the page's one attractive figure and its one unattributed one, and leaving the caption undeclared is now the mechanism enforcing the warning above rather than a sentence asking to be remembered.
what_it_supplies: an 1857 statement, independent of Andreas and of Wentworth, that the fort was occupied from 1832 until 1836
the demolition sequence: the principal buildings in summer 1856, the block-house weeks later
the existence and titling of Henry Hart's 1853 survey, 'Fort Dearborn, City of Chicago, Surveyed and Published by Henry Hart, Civil Engineer and Architect, New York'
what_it_does_not_supply: any attribution for the dimensioned woodcut caption, which is the only place a fort measurement appears on the page
any dimension of the stockade itself
the fort as it stood in 1835 — every view it reproduces is 1850 or later
